Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
At 40, Alejandro Morales had spent years training himself to stay steady in emergencies. As a surgeon, he was used to alarms, urgency, and the expectation that his hands should remain precise while other people panicked. What happened during a wildfire in the hills outside his California community did not fit into that professional identity in any way he could master. He and his wife had been at home when the air changed first, a dry, dirty smell pushing through the windows before they could fully understand the danger. Then came the noise: heavy crashing sounds from outside, the crack of trees and fencing giving way, the erratic percussion of helicopters overhead, sirens, shouted instructions, and bursts that sounded close enough to be inside the house. He remembered moving quickly through rooms, trying to gather a few things, and he remembered the burnt smell thickening until it seemed to coat the back of his throat. But when he tried to tell the story afterward, Alejandro found that he could only retrieve fragments. He could picture his wife’s face in the strange orange light, the sound of something exploding or collapsing nearby, the sensation of heat and smoke, and then the memory seemed to break apart. Large sections felt simply absent, as if the event had been torn into pieces and some had never been returned.

In the weeks after the fire, he noticed that the memory did not come to him gradually. It arrived all at once, with no warning, pulled into the present by ordinary things in a way that made him feel ambushed by his own surroundings. A slammed metal door in the hospital, a dropped instrument tray, construction banging outside the surgical wing—any loud noise could bring back the whole scene in an instant, not as a story he was recalling but as a full rush of sound, heat, and alarm. The smell of smoke was even worse. If a resident came in from outside after standing near someone smoking, if there was a faint electrical burnt odor in an operating room, if food charred in the hospital cafeteria, he felt his body lock onto it immediately. Burnt smells seemed especially potent because they matched what he remembered most clearly from that day: not a clean campfire scent, but the acrid, alarming smell that told him something was being consumed and might spread.

When the memory hit, what overtook him was not only fear but grief so intense it felt almost out of proportion to whatever was happening in the present moment. He would become flooded with a sense of terrible loss and helplessness, sometimes needing a few minutes alone before he could re-enter a case or speak normally to colleagues. He struggled to explain this to himself. He knew his house had not been the only one threatened, knew that others had lost more, yet whenever the memory broke through, he felt the grief as though he were standing again at the edge of something irretrievable.

Over time Alejandro developed ways of getting through the day that made sense to him in the moment. He kept himself relentlessly occupied, flipping on a podcast during his commute, scrolling through medical updates late at night, volunteering for extra administrative tasks between surgeries—anything that might prevent his mind from going quiet enough for the fragments to gather. After difficult days he drank more than he used to, telling himself it was just to take the edge off and sleep. On some nights he also took medication or used alcohol specifically because he did not want to lie awake waiting for some random sound or smell to bring the fire back. He was ashamed of how often sexual fantasies became another form of release for him, a fast way to discharge tension without having to think or speak. He did not describe these habits as helping so much as interrupting; they gave him brief stretches in which he did not have to feel cornered by the next reminder.

These patterns began to affect his life at home and at work. His wife noticed that he seemed present and absent at once, physically there but quick to redirect conversations, restless whenever the apartment filled with cooking smells, irritable when a neighbor set off fireworks or when city noise echoed unexpectedly at night. At the hospital he remained technically excellent, but he started timing his breaks to avoid the loading dock area where diesel exhaust and overheated machinery sometimes created a burnt odor. Once, after a loud crash in a nearby corridor, he froze just long enough in the scrub room that a colleague asked if he was ill. Alejandro brushed it off, embarrassed by how little control he felt over something so immediate and sensory.

He sought help only after a recent evening when his wife burned food on the stove and the smell rolled through the kitchen. Before he could orient himself, the full memory was there again, broken images and overwhelming grief arriving together so forcefully that he had to leave the apartment and stand outside. Seeing how frightened and confused his wife was afterward unsettled him more than his own reaction. He came in for treatment wanting, above all, to stop feeling as if his surroundings could seize him without warning. What frightened him most was not simply remembering the wildfire, but the sense that the memory remained incomplete, waiting in pieces around him, ready to return through any loud noise or burnt smell at any moment.
